## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷahaṁsajātaka* (Ja 533), titled *The Shorter Tale of the Golden Goose*, is a canonical Pali birth story belonging to the Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to its traditional frame narrative set at the Bamboo Grove, the Buddha related the tale after the venerable Ānanda offered his life to protect the Buddha when Devadatta unleashed a mad elephant; the Buddha explained that Ānanda had similarly demonstrated unflinching self-sacrifice on his behalf across four past lives [SuttaCentral; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a king of golden geese who is captured by a fowler [Anandajoti 2010]. His loyal commander-in-chief, Sumukha, refuses to abandon him despite permission to flee, and both are brought before the human king, who is so impressed by their nobility and virtue that he grants them their release [Anandajoti 2010; Buddhaghosa 1921].

The text is cited in late canonical and commentarial exegesis; for instance, Buddhaghosa’s *Atthasālinī* quotes a verse addressed to Sumukha from the Jātaka to illustrate color classifications and the semantic range of the term *hari* [Buddhaghosa 1921]. Computational text-reuse analysis in DharmaNexus identifies significant verse and segment correspondences with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as closely related geese legends such as the *Mahāhaṁsajātaka* (Ja 534) and another *Cūḷahaṁsajātaka* (Ja 502) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments demonstrate textual and narrative counterparts in Āryaśūra’s Sanskrit *Jātakamālā* (and its Tibetan translation), the *Saṅghabhedavastu* of the Vinaya, and Kṣemendra’s *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* [DharmaNexus].
